samples: This program prints a directory tree, starting at the folder given as the first command-line argument (or the current folder). Each line shows an entry's name, indented two spaces per level, with its total size in bytes. A folder's size is the sum of everything beneath it, and children are listed in name order. It only reads the filesystem and writes to the console, and it stops with a file error at the first entry it cannot read. Because it re-measures every subfolder at each level, it will be slow on very large trees. It also uses filesystem operations (inspecting an entry, getting a path's name) that the documented library list doesn't include, so confirm they exist before relying on it.

This program prints a directory tree, starting at the first command-line argument or the current directory. Each file and folder appears on its own line, indented by depth and sorted by name within its folder, with its size in bytes; a folder's size is the sum of everything beneath it, and anything that is neither file nor folder counts as zero. It only reads the filesystem and stops at the first error, but it re-measures every subfolder at each level, so it will be slow on large trees, and it relies on a few filesystem operations (inspecting an entry, getting a path's name) that the documented library doesn't list, so check they exist before depending on it.

This program prints a directory tree, starting at the folder given on the command line or the current folder if none is given. Each line shows a file or folder name, indented two spaces per level and sorted by name within each folder, followed by its size in bytes, where a folder's size is the total of everything beneath it. It only reads the filesystem and stops at the first error, but it re-measures every subfolder at each level, so it will be slow on very large trees. It also relies on a few filesystem features (inspecting an entry, getting a path's name, the entry and error types) that the documented library doesn't list, so check that they exist before depending on it.

This program prints a directory tree, starting at the folder given on the command line or the current folder, with each file and folder indented by depth and followed by its size in bytes. Folder sizes are the sum of everything beneath them, children are printed in name order, and any filesystem error stops the run with a failure. Before relying on it, note that it only needs read access to the filesystem and the console, but it recomputes sizes from scratch at every level, so large trees will be slow. It also uses filesystem features (inspecting an entry, the entry type, getting a path's name) that the documented standard library doesn't list, so check they exist before depending on it.

This program prints a directory tree, starting from the folder named as the first command-line argument (or the current folder if none is given). Each entry appears on its own line, indented by depth, with its total size in bytes (folders count everything beneath them) and children sorted by name. It only reads the filesystem and writes to the console, and it stops with a file error on the first failure. It also re-measures every subfolder's contents at each level, so it will be slow on very large trees, and it relies on a filesystem inspection feature that isn't in the library list I know, so I can't confirm that part works.
